headline: A US Census Bureau working paper estimates that graduates of the most AI-exposed majors have been 5 percentage points less likely to be employed and earned 13 per cent less in their first full quarter since ChatGPT launched.
score_reason: Lowered by 2 from 5: the paper dates from September 2026 and was reported on 22 Sep 2026, so the 16 Oct Campus Reform article repeats old news, and it is a working paper.
importance_line: Recent graduates in fields such as computer science, accounting, journalism and engineering may face weaker first jobs and pay, universities and employers may need to rethink entry-level paths, and it is one working paper whose authors cannot yet say how long the gap lasts or prove AI alone caused it.
summary: Economists Cody Orr, Lee C. Tucker and Lawrence Warren, writing for the US Census Bureau's Center for Economic Studies, report in a September 2026 working paper (early research, with no outside review reported) that in their adjusted estimates the 10 per cent of college majors most exposed to AI saw the chance of employment right after graduation fall by 5 percentage points and first full-quarter earnings fall by 13 per cent, a loss they compare to graduating into a large recession. About half the earnings drop comes from lower pay within industries and the rest from graduates moving into lower-paying sectors such as restaurants and retail, and the effects shrink as graduates gain experience but remain substantial.
notes: Pool item came from Campus Reform (16 Oct 2026), whose page was blocked (Vercel security check, HTTP 429), so it was not read. Found the Census Bureau's own page for working paper CES-WP-26-56 'Graduating into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors' (September 2026; page posted about 9 to 10 Sep) and Inside Higher Ed's report of 22 Sep 2026 (computer science, accounting, journalism and engineering among the most exposed; nursing and education among the least). Streamline Feed (Kenya, 12 Oct) gives the paper's date as 1 Sep and adds that the comparison group is the bottom six deciles and that the series notice says working papers are not Bureau-reviewed publications; those two points were not checked on census.gov. Old news by about six weeks; suggest NO OLD NEWS drop.
